{"id": "19:17/q13", "question": "Is assimilation read in 'fa-tamaththala lahā'?", "turns_on": "Which sound Ruways transmission is followed; both assimilation and clear articulation are reported.", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q13/p1", "position": "Ruways assimilates the adjacent sounds in this phrase in one sound transmission.", "reasons": "Al-Dānī and Ibn al-Faḥḥām transmit the assimilation here and in wa-li-tuṣnaʿa ʿalayya; al-Tadhkira and al-Mabhaj list both. Ibn al-Jazarī places this among fourteen optional Ruways assimilation sites across several sūras."}, {"id": "19:17/q13/p2", "position": "Ruways also has a sound transmission with clear pronunciation here.", "reasons": "Other transmitters preserve clear pronunciation across the listed passages; Ibn al-Jazarī accepts both transmissions."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q14", "question": "Could Mary have been a prophetess?", "turns_on": "Whether an angelic mission and conversation establish prophethood, despite the lack of explicit designation and the usual male-prophet tradition.", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q14/p1", "position": "Yes; the divine mission and angel's conversation suggest prophethood.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers it; Abū Ḥayyān treats the wording as apparent evidence. Ibn Ḥazm and Rūzbihān add that named Qur'anic figures are generally prophets (12:109)."}, {"id": "19:17/q14/p2", "position": "No; an angel may speak in human form to a person who is not a prophet.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān compares Gabriel appearing as Diḥya and in the report about Islam and faith. Most authorities say the Qur'an never explicitly calls Mary a prophet and tradition generally holds prophets male; they rank her instead among the most pious women (12:109)."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q15", "question": "Can an angel of immense size appear as a human-sized body?", "turns_on": "Whether manifestation changes Gabriel's actual bodily dimensions or presents an unchanged angel through human perception.", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q15/p1", "position": "Yes; essential bodily parts may be few, or a spiritual being may assume bodies of different sizes.", "reasons": "Rāzī answers the objection that losing parts destroys Gabriel and overlapping them is impossible by distinguishing essential from additional bodily parts, or spiritual from bodily existence."}, {"id": "19:17/q15/p2", "position": "The objection fails because the verse describes an appearance to Mary, not bodily transformation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects Rāzī's physical answer for presupposing a transformation; Gabriel remained an angel perceived in human shape. He compares Satan appearing as Surāqa at Badr (8:48), other reported appearances, and dream figures without independent visible bodies."}, {"id": "19:17/q15/p3", "position": "A huge body cannot become human-sized without destructive loss or impossible overlapping parts.", "reasons": "This objection is recorded by Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī as an argument put to the exegetes."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q16", "question": "Does angelic human appearance undermine certainty that a person seen twice is the same?", "turns_on": "Whether recognition rests directly on sensation or on tested inference from sensory images, and whether a possible impersonation defeats ordinary certainty.", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q16/p1", "position": "It could: an angel, jinn, or duplicate might impersonate the known person.", "reasons": "Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī record the example of Zayd seen on two days; the objection says sensory recognition alone would invite skepticism."}, {"id": "19:17/q16/p2", "position": "The possibility is already present if God can create an exact duplicate or naturalists' rare conjunctions occur.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the objection is not specific to angels, since a freely acting Creator or planetary conjunction could yield the same apparent duplicate. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects an added reply that such duplicates are rare because its rarity could not be established."}, {"id": "19:17/q16/p3", "position": "Sensation supplies an image; reason and tested experience judge the external person's identity.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites shifts of apparent size, direction, motion and the sun's size, fear-produced images and mirages. The sensed image is certain as an experience, while external identification requires thought and evidence; this does not abolish trust in the senses. He rejects the unproven 'rare duplicate' reply."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q17", "question": "Does human manifestation imply that angels could appear as insects or other animals?", "turns_on": "Whether one reported human manifestation entails animal forms, and whether revelation establishes their nonoccurrence.", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q17/p1", "position": "Yes, as an alleged absurd consequence of allowing human form.", "reasons": "Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī record this third objection."}, {"id": "19:17/q17/p2", "position": "Reason allows the possibility, but reliable revelation establishes that such cases do not occur.", "reasons": "Rāzī answers the objection by separating intellectual possibility from divinely reported actuality."}, {"id": "19:17/q17/p3", "position": "Human appearance does not entail animal appearance, and bare possibility is harmless.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the appeal to revelation because he finds no reliable scriptural proof excluding animal forms."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q18", "question": "Does angelic impersonation undermine mass-transmitted reports?", "turns_on": "Whether revelation or tested inference can secure the identity of figures known through sensory reports.", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q18/p1", "position": "It could, since the person at Badr might be an impersonator rather than Muhammad.", "reasons": "Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī record this fourth objection."}, {"id": "19:17/q18/p2", "position": "Reliable revelation rules out appearances that would unsettle transmitted certainty.", "reasons": "Rāzī gives this answer, alongside his answer about insect form; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that revelation itself comes through hearing and would face the same uncertainty."}, {"id": "19:17/q18/p3", "position": "Ordinary confidence rests on reason and tested experience interpreting sensory images.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī applies his account of perception to transmitted reports and rejects circular reliance on revelation; appearances of Satan as Surāqa at Badr and other figures show that a real being can present a familiar image."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q19", "question": "What does Mary's response to the visitor show?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q19/p1", "position": "Her immediate appeal for refuge displays exceptional chastity and piety.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī treats the handsome visitor as a test; Iṣlāḥī says the unexpected divine encounter showed unmatched character. Al-Ālūsī uses the next verse's refuge to reject the proposal that she was aroused."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q20", "question": "What practice was associated with Mary's screen?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q20/p1", "position": "Christians use screens at altars and ritual sites because Mary screened herself.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this explanation to ʿUmar."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q21", "question": "How was Mary's eastern withdrawal linked to prayer direction or symbolism?", "turns_on": "Whether east has a historical prayer association or a symbolic relation to Jesus; al-Ālūsī doubts the latter.", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q21/p1", "position": "Reports connect Christian eastward prayer to Mary's eastern retreat, while her eastward direction may have been incidental.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī also records a report that Christians faced Jerusalem during Jesus' life; Bursawī reports al-Ḥasan's contrast of Christians facing east and Jews west because the Torah meeting occurred on the mountain's western side (28:44)."}, {"id": "19:17/q21/p2", "position": "The physical sunrise in the east prefigured Jesus as spiritual light.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records this proposed symbolism but calls it far-fetched."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q22", "question": "How does this story connect to the surrounding sūra and prior sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q22/p1", "position": "The sūras join accounts of astonishing births and events; John's birth prepares for Jesus' birth.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān compares al-Kahf's Cave, Moses and Khiḍr, and Dhū al-Qarnayn with John's birth to old and barren parents and Jesus' birth without a father (18:9, 60, 83). Iṣlāḥī says John was Jesus' predecessor and relative, making Christians reconsider deifying one of two consecutive prophets in the same family."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q23", "question": "Where was Sūrat Maryam revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q23/p1", "position": "The sūra is Meccan, with a reported Medinan exception for its prostration verse.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says it is Meccan like the prior sūra; Muqātil places the prostration verse in Medina after migration to Abyssinia."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q24", "question": "What is the veil in the inward reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q24/p1", "position": "The sanctuary of holiness, separated from the soul's world by the chest and the limits of material perception.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the Holy Spirit could be sent only after Mary rose through detachment into the holy world."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q25", "question": "How does the inward reading explain the Spirit's effect on Mary's body?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q25/p1", "position": "Holy Spirit and imagined human form act through the heart, animal and natural souls to comfort and alter Mary's bodily powers.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī likens revelation to true dreams with quiet bodily faculties; images of the rational soul and holy spirits pass into the body, stirring desire and conception. He adds that Spirit's support can change temperament beyond proportion."}]}

us' extraordinary birth lead some followers to claim?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q26/p1", "position": "Some followers deified Jesus despite his call to worship God alone.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the extraordinary miracle prompted this misdirection."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q27", "question": "How is Muhammad's mission contrasted with disputes over Jesus?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q27/p1", "position": "After centuries of dispute, God chose a final messenger who was fully human and shared ordinary human needs.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites 25:7 and presents this as following the disputes over Jesus' nature."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q28", "question": "What is the great sign of Muhammad's prophethood in this comparison?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q28/p1", "position": "The Qur'an, a clear Arabic book the Arabs could not match.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ frames her study around this sign."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q29", "question": "Did the Muʿtazilites deny miracles other than the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "Whether declining to use unseen reports in later debate amounts to denying the miracles themselves.", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q29/p1", "position": "No; they affirmed other miracles as proofs but did not rely in debate on reports unavailable to later audiences.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ explicitly rejects the claim of wholesale denial."}, {"id": "19:17/q29/p2", "position": "They denied all miracles other than the Qur'an.", "reasons": "This is the claim Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q30", "question": "How does Islam relate to earlier revelations in this account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q30/p1", "position": "It confirms and safeguards their truth and completes the prophetic message as humanity matures in responsibility.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connects this to Muhammad's final mission."}]}
{"id": "19:17/q31", "question": "What action preceded Mary's taking a screen?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:17/q31/p1", "position": "Mary withdrew from her people.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī explains intabadhat in the preceding verse as form VIII of n-b-dh, 'to cast aside.'"}]}
{"id": "19:22/q01", "question": "What does “she carried him” say Mary conceived?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q01/p1", "position": "Mary became pregnant with Jesus.", "reasons": "Al-Damghani explains ḥaml as pregnancy ending at delivery; Ibn al-Jawzi identifies the object as Jesus."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q02", "question": "How did Mary conceive Jesus?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over the breather, the path of the breath, and what bodily process made conception possible.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q02/p1", "position": "Gabriel's breath entered through her garment opening or collar and reached her womb.", "reasons": "Yahya's report has Gabriel draw the opening with his finger; Wahb says he appeared as a man and breathed there, sometimes after Mary accepted God's command. Al-Suddi describes the front slit and chest; Ibn Jurayj names neckline and sleeve. Ibn Abbas says she felt pregnancy at once. Al-Baqir says the fetus instantly became complete and Mary felt its weight. Alusi reads the explanatory fāʾ as implying her trust. Ibn Kathir says conception occurred by God's permission; 21:91 and 66:12 are cited for the Spirit's breath. Reports vary between edge, collar, split neckline and the garment being put on afterward."}, {"id": "19:22/q02/p2", "position": "Gabriel's breath entered through her sleeve.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj names both neckline and sleeve; al-Suddi says it entered Mary's chest through the sleeve. Other compilers list the sleeve alongside other reported openings."}, {"id": "19:22/q02/p3", "position": "Gabriel's breath entered through the garment's lower hem.", "reasons": "Razi reports a view that the breath traveled from the hem to the womb; Alusi also lists the hem among the reported entry points."}, {"id": "19:22/q02/p4", "position": "Gabriel's breath entered Mary's mouth.", "reasons": "Razi reports that it reached her belly and caused immediate conception; other compilers also list the mouth."}, {"id": "19:22/q02/p5", "position": "Gabriel breathed from a distance and the breath reached Mary.", "reasons": "Baghawi says the wind reached her and conception followed immediately; Alusi reports that Gabriel did not approach."}, {"id": "19:22/q02/p6", "position": "God Himself breathed the spirit.", "reasons": "Razi reports the appeal to wording about God's spirit and the analogy with Adam in 3:59 and 15:29; he notes that wording about breathing into Jesus can refer to Mary because Jesus was in her womb."}, {"id": "19:22/q02/p7", "position": "The one who spoke to Mary was the child she carried, who entered through her mouth.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports this from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb."}, {"id": "19:22/q02/p8", "position": "Jesus formed bodily from Mary's fluid after Gabriel's human appearance stirred her.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the human appearance preserved a human pattern; Mary's pleasure and imagined fluid entered the womb. He invokes Jesus' reviving miracles as reflecting Gabriel's breath, and rejects naturalists who deny generation from one parent's fluid. He says a mother's state or sight at conception can shape her child; Mary's calm after the angelic good news, 3:45, made Jesus open-hearted. Breath need not enter by an opening, as Adam's spirit entered through his crown."}, {"id": "19:22/q02/p9", "position": "Jesus' spirit joined semen only after it settled in the womb and became ready.", "reasons": "Qashani says the settled semen first united into a temperament able to receive the spirit."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q03", "question": "What event is left unstated between the angel's speech and Mary's pregnancy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q03/p1", "position": "God decreed it, Gabriel breathed into Mary, and she conceived.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says the omission is clear from other Quranic passages because the Quran is one book; Razi supplies the decree and Gabriel's breath."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q04", "question": "How old was Mary when she conceived?", "turns_on": "Competing age reports; Razi says the Quran supplies no decisive age.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q04/p1", "position": "Thirteen years old.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Atiyya and Bursevi report thirteen; reports collected by Kashshaf, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, Nasafi and Baydawi include it. Razi cautions that the Quran establishes no age."}, {"id": "19:22/q04/p2", "position": "Ten years old.", "reasons": "Muqatil's age appears in Thalabi and Baghawi; Baydawi couples it with two menstrual periods. Other compilers list ten among conflicting ages."}, {"id": "19:22/q04/p3", "position": "Fifteen years old.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi attribute this report to Wahb and Mujahid."}, {"id": "19:22/q04/p4", "position": "Fourteen years old.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi list this among the reports."}, {"id": "19:22/q04/p5", "position": "Twelve years old.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi list this among the reports."}, {"id": "19:22/q04/p6", "position": "Twenty years old.", "reasons": "Razi and Nasafi report it; Razi says the Quran fixes none of the reported ages."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q05", "question": "Had Mary menstruated before conceiving?", "turns_on": "The reports distinguish two prior periods, no period yet, and no menstruation ever.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q05/p1", "position": "She had menstruated twice.", "reasons": "Muqatil and later compilers pair two periods with differing ages, ten or thirteen; Razi says the Quran establishes none of these details."}, {"id": "19:22/q05/p2", "position": "She had not yet menstruated.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan lists this report against the two-period and never-menstruated accounts; Alusi notes the disagreement without specifying the alternative."}, {"id": "19:22/q05/p3", "position": "She never menstruated.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this as a third account of Mary's menstrual history."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q06", "question": "How long did Mary carry Jesus before his birth?", "turns_on": "Conflicting transmitted durations and whether the consecutive fāʾ clauses imply immediate birth or allow ordinary stages; Abu Hayyan says the reports contradict one another and should be left aside.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q06/p1", "position": "Nine months, the ordinary duration.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan, Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Saʾib, the majority according to Ibn Kathir, and reports attributed to Ibn Abbas and al-Baqir support it. Ibn Kathir prefers ordinary development: the fāʾ permits intervals, stages of human creation are each forty days in sound reports and 23:12–14, and 22:63 likewise joins rain to later greening. Alusi inclines to nine months though he considers the reports unsound and the instantaneous argument inconclusive. Samarrai says each fāʾ event follows after its natural interval. Kuranyolu cites Ibn Kathir's majority report."}, {"id": "19:22/q06/p2", "position": "An hour or no extended interval separated conception and birth.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas appeals to the uninterrupted Quranic sequence; Qurtubi calls that the apparent reading, and Bursevi cites both the fāʾ and Jesus' direct creation. Razi adduces the divine 'Be' analogy with Adam in 3:59 and says ordinary gestational intervals pertain to semen. Muqatil's shorter scheme differs: conception, formation and nursing each in an hour. Ibn al-Jawzi says immediate birth cannot be literal because Mary withdrew while carrying him; Ibn Kathir calls the report strange and Alusi finds the inference inconclusive. Alusi also says no duration report is sound."}, {"id": "19:22/q06/p3", "position": "Six months.", "reasons": "Listed by Thalabi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Ibn al-Jawzi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Tabatabai; Alusi says naturalists give six months as a minimum."}, {"id": "19:22/q06/p4", "position": "Eight months.", "reasons": "Several
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

<<chunk 79, part 2 of 0..5>>
 sources call Jesus the only surviving eight-month infant, making his survival a sign; Ikrima says an eight-month child ordinarily does not live. Alusi rejects astrological explanations based on planetary months as fables."}, {"id": "19:22/q06/p5", "position": "Three hours, one each for conception, formation, and birth.", "reasons": "Muqatil's sequence puts the birth at noon; reports vary as to whether the separate hours describe forming, nursing, or birth. Thalabi, Kashshaf, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan relay versions."}, {"id": "19:22/q06/p6", "position": "Seven months.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Abu Hayyan attribute seven months to ʿAtaʾ, Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Dahhak; Baydawi, Nasafi and Alusi also list it."}, {"id": "19:22/q06/p7", "position": "Nine hours, with delivery on the same day.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi attributes this to al-Hasan; Tabatabai reports it from Imam al-Sadiq."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q07", "question": "What does the sequence of fāʾ clauses imply about timing?", "turns_on": "Whether consecutive clauses specify a short elapsed time or merely the order of events.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q07/p1", "position": "Each event follows the previous one, while the interval depends on the event.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares human developmental stages in 23:12–14 and land greening after rain in 22:63; Samarrai says normal pregnancy can intervene without breaking succession. Ibn Ashur says conception followed the exchange closely, while the fāʾ expresses consequence. Ibn al-Jawzi says Mary still carried Jesus during withdrawal. Alusi finds immediate birth unproved."}, {"id": "19:22/q07/p2", "position": "The immediate sequence suggests a very short interval.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas draws immediate birth from the sequence; Tabrisi infers just an hour between Mary's withdrawal and conception; Qurtubi calls immediate birth the more apparent reading. Bursevi adds Jesus' direct creation and the fāʾ. Biqai reads the fāʾ as immediate withdrawal with the child in her womb."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q08", "question": "When did Mary withdraw?", "turns_on": "Whether the narrative's sequence places departure at awareness of pregnancy or near delivery.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q08/p1", "position": "She withdrew after recognizing she was pregnant.", "reasons": "Wahidi Wajiz says she sensed pregnancy; Nasafi and Ibn Kathir likewise make discovery of pregnancy precede departure. Biqai takes fāʾ to mark immediate withdrawal; Kuranyolu says she concealed the pregnancy for a time."}, {"id": "19:22/q08/p2", "position": "She withdrew as birth approached.", "reasons": "Wahidi Basit reads the sequence as departure at delivery; al-Suddi says she went east as delivery approached. Wahb's account has God direct her to leave near birth; Bursevi reports her leaving Zakariya's house at night then. Nawf describes heaviness and labor pains before flight."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q09", "question": "What does “with him” describe in her withdrawal?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q09/p1", "position": "The bāʾ expresses accompaniment or state: she withdrew while carrying Jesus in her womb.", "reasons": "Kashshaf cites a poetic line and 23:20 on a plant bearing oil; Razi repeats the plant comparison. Baydawi and Samin cite poetry; Samin identifies the phrase as circumstantial. Bursevi calls it accompaniment or state; Alusi cites 6:99. Zajjaj glosses going away with the child, while Ibn Ashur says ḥamalat bihi can stress close attachment and cites Abu Kabir al-Hudhali and 46:15."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q10", "question": "Why did Mary withdraw from her people?", "turns_on": "Reports give fear of accusation, concern for others' embarrassment, and protection of the child; Razi says the text does not choose among them.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q10/p1", "position": "She feared blame or an accusation of wrongdoing for bearing a child without a husband.", "reasons": "Muqatil says she went beyond the hills, away from family. Qushayri says she had no trusted confidant. Wahidi says she feared reproach from Zechariah and her people; Baghawi identifies shame over no husband. Ibn Atiyya emphasizes modesty; Tabrisi says shame and accusation, including her aunt failing to recognize her. Ibn Kathir says she hid from people's sight; Ibn Ishaq says they accused her and Yusuf when pregnancy became visible. Abu Hayyan, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Kuranyolu and others give the same fear."}, {"id": "19:22/q10/p2", "position": "She left to protect the child from danger.", "reasons": "Wahb says God told Mary to leave lest her people shame her and kill the child; Razi lists fear for the child's safety while saying the text chooses no reason. Alusi relays Wahb's command near birth. Study Quran includes protection of both Mary and the child."}, {"id": "19:22/q10/p3", "position": "She wished to spare Zechariah embarrassment.", "reasons": "Razi lists this among reasons but says the text chooses none; Study Quran connects the concern with protecting Mary and the child from misunderstanding."}, {"id": "19:22/q10/p4", "position": "She felt shame because of her known piety.", "reasons": "Razi lists this separately and says the verse itself does not choose a reason; Ibn Atiyya stresses modesty."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q11", "question": "Where was the distant place?", "turns_on": "The reports identify different sites; the verse specifies remoteness but, as Ibn Ashur says, does not name a place.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q11/p1", "position": "Near Bethlehem, at or beyond the far end of its valley.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas names the far end of the Valley of Bethlehem; Ibn Atiyya says Bethlehem is four miles from Jerusalem, while Kashifi gives about six miles from Iliya and Ibn al-Jawzi reports six miles walked. Bursevi cites the Isra report from Anas: Gabriel said he prayed at Bethlehem, where Jesus was born, a report Bursevi calls authentic or hasan and attributes to al-Nasaʾi and al-Bayhaqi. Ibn Ashur appeals to Luke's Bethlehem birth against an Egypt birth."}, {"id": "19:22/q11/p2", "position": "At the far eastern side of the sanctuary or near the Temple.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi locates it there as delivery approached; Nawf says Mary fled east in embarrassment. Study Quran mentions an eastern Temple identification but prefers a place where Mary was unknown."}, {"id": "19:22/q11/p3", "position": "Behind a mountain or beyond the hills.", "reasons": "Muqatil says away from family beyond hills; Kashshaf, Razi, Nasafi and Alusi mention a mountain. Kashifi locates a mountain or valley near Bethlehem; Abu Hayyan reports a birth behind a mountain."}, {"id": "19:22/q11/p4", "position": "At the far end of her house or in its farthest room.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi and Abu Hayyan report the house; Bursevi's cited Irshad and Alusi prefer the far side or farthest room because it fits a short pregnancy."}, {"id": "19:22/q11/p5", "position": "In Egypt or nearby, with Joseph helping her flee.", "reasons": "Wahb's report in Ibn Atiyya says Egypt or a nearby region; Alusi says Joseph carried her toward Egypt and labor began there. Study Quran reports a later flight with Joseph as delivery approached. Ibn Ashur rejects an Egypt birth because Luke places it at Bethlehem and 19:27 has Mary return carrying Jesus."}, {"id": "19:22/q11/p6", "position": "Outside Jerusalem after leaving Zechariah's house.", "reasons": "A story cited by Bursevi has her leave at night as birth approached, wishing Zechariah and others not to know."}, {"id": "19:22/q11/p7", "position": "A remote place away from family, without a specified site.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the verse offers no grounds to choose a particular place; Study Quran prefers a place where Mary was unknown over the Temple vicinity. Tabatabai says she separated from her people."}]}
{"id": "19:22/q12", "question": "What does qaṣiyyan mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q12/p1", "position": "Far away or remote.", "reasons": "Al-Farra compares qaṣiyyan with qāṣiyan and cites an anonymous poem using al-qaṣiyy for distance; Tabari and Wahidi cite a rajaz line and the root meaning to become or make distant. Zajjaj says both forms mean distant. Tabrisi contrasts it with near; Ibn Ashur says it derives from distance."}]}

{"id": "19:22/q21", "question": "What inward sense is given to Mary's distant withdrawal?", "turns_on": "The two inward readings address different spiritual aspects of Mary's experience.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q21/p1", "position": "She moved from the eastern place into the western natural and bodily horizon with the child.", "reasons": "Qashani identifies the west with natural bodily existence."}, {"id": "19:22/q21/p2", "position": "Her ordeal is a trial that burns away blameworthy dispositions and yields divine qualities through patience.", "reasons": "Bursevi presents this spiritual reading of her trial."}]}

{"id": "19:22/q23", "question": "Where and when was this surah revealed?", "turns_on": "Whether the surah's Meccan classification has an exception for its prostration verse.", "positions": [{"id": "19:22/q23/p1", "position": "The surah is Meccan like the preceding surah.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan states this general classification."}, {"id": "19:22/q23/p2", "position": "Muqatil excludes the prostration verse, placing its revelation in Medina after the migration to Abyssinia.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports Muqatil's exception to the surah's Meccan classification."}]}
{"id": "19:24/q01", "question": "Who called Mary from beneath her?", "turns_on": "Whether the newborn's immediate speech and Mary's later gesture identify the caller, or Gabriel called from a lower place; the readings alone do not settle it for all commentators.", "positions": [{"id": "19:24/q01/p1", "position": "The caller was Jesus, speaking as a newborn beneath Mary.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Wahb, Saʿīd, Ubayy and others transmit this. {"id": "19:24/q02", "question": "How is مِن تَحْتِهَآ read and construed?", "turns_on": "The vowel and case of min/man and taḥtihā, and how strongly either reading fixes the identity of the caller.", "positions": [{"id": "19:24/q02/p1", "position": "With kasra, min is a preposition and taḥtihā is genitive: 'from beneath her.'", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid, al-Nashr and Ibn ʿĀshūr enumerate the readers, with some variations in lists. {"id": "19:24/q10", "question": "What does سَرِيًّۭا mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether Arabic usage, poetry and the eat-and-drink context establish a watercourse, or the word denotes a noble person; reports also disagree on whose nobility is meant.", "positions": [{"id": "19:24/q10/p1", "position": "A small river, stream, channel or spring of flowing water was supplied to Mary.", "reasons": "The majority and Arabic linguists give this sense.
